passage: Amandeep, you're afraid to speak at tomorrow's meeting because you might stumble? Sit with your Farida Aapa for a minute. When I was a young woman, in my first job at the bank in Aligarh, I stayed silent in every Monday meeting for six months. I was sure that if I said one wrong number, the whole branch would remember it for years. Then one evening I asked myself a strange question: what do I remember of other people's mistakes in those meetings? I tried hard. Nothing. Not one. I couldn't even remember who had mixed up the dates the week before, and I had been sitting right there. Everyone was busy with their own worries, just like me. So I gave myself permission to be a little wrong. The next Monday I spoke. My voice shook. Nobody noticed. By Tuesday nobody remembered.

qa.q: How long did Farida Aapa stay silent in the Monday meetings?
qa.a: For six months.

qa.q: What was young Farida feeling during those silent months?
qa.a: She felt anxious and self-conscious, sure one wrong number would be remembered by the whole branch for years.

qa.q: Which moment in the story changed things for young Farida?
qa.a: Asking herself what she remembered of others' mistakes and finding nothing, which let her give herself permission to speak imperfectly.

qa.q: How did the others at the meeting respond when young Farida finally spoke?
qa.a: Nobody noticed her shaking voice, and by Tuesday nobody remembered, because they were busy with their own worries.

grounding: An elder recalls realising she remembered nothing of others' slips, seeing that people are self-focused, and letting herself speak imperfectly.

passage: The wedding hall in Jaipur was deafening: the band outside, children shrieking, the DJ testing speakers. Vasudha had been asked, twenty minutes before, to give a short toast for her best friend. She hadn't prepared. Her hands were cold. What if she forgot a name, or her voice cracked, and everyone remembered it for the rest of the wedding? Saurabh, the groom's cousin, saw her face. "You okay?" "What if I mess up?" He laughed. "Name one thing anyone got wrong in last night's speeches." Vasudha tried. The uncle who spoke too long? She couldn't remember what he'd said. The aunt whose mic cut out? She wasn't even sure which aunt. "See," Saurabh said. "Nobody's keeping score." Vasudha took the mic. She said the bride's childhood nickname wrong, laughed, corrected it, and carried on. Nobody mentioned it again.

qa.q: How long before the toast was Vasudha asked to give it?
qa.a: Twenty minutes before.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling before taking the mic?
qa.a: She felt nervous and anxious, hands cold, afraid a small slip would be remembered by everyone for the rest of the wedding.

qa.q: What helped Vasudha speak despite the noise and the short notice?
qa.a: Recalling that she remembered almost nothing of last night's speech mistakes, which showed her people are self-focused, so she let herself be imperfect.

qa.q: How does Saurabh see the idea of messing up a toast?
qa.a: Saurabh sees it as no big deal, since nobody keeps score of other people's small slips.

grounding: Shows a young professional under time pressure realising she remembers little of others' slips, and giving herself permission to speak imperfectly.

passage: In the Chennai office, Usha had avoided presenting at the Friday demo for months. The one time she had tried, in March, she'd called the client by the wrong name and wanted to disappear. This Friday her manager, Vishal, put her on the list anyway. On Thursday night, lying awake, Usha made herself answer a question: what did she remember about anyone else's mistakes at those demos? She knew people had made them. Someone's laptop had crashed once. Someone had laughed at the wrong moment. But who? When? She truly couldn't say. So maybe nobody remembered her March either. She wrote on a sticky note: "Be clear, not perfect." On Friday she presented. Her slide froze once, and she said, "Give me a second," and it was fine. Afterwards Vishal said only, "Good point about the delivery times."

qa.q: What did Usha write on the sticky note?
qa.a: Be clear, not perfect.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling on Thursday night?
qa.a: She felt anxious and ashamed, still haunted by calling the client the wrong name in March.

qa.q: Which question helped Usha, and why?
qa.a: Asking what she remembered of other people's demo mistakes; realising she couldn't recall them showed her that others were also focused on themselves.

qa.q: How did Vishal seem to see Usha's presentation?
qa.a: Vishal focused on her content, praising her point about delivery times, and didn't mention the frozen slide.

grounding: Shows a young professional asking how much she remembers of others' slips, realising people are self-focused, and giving herself permission to be imperfect.

passage: On the Diwali party day at the playschool, Sudha miss brought out the big snakes-and-ladders mat. Neelam held the huge foam dice in both hands. She squeezed her eyes shut, blew on it three times, and whispered, "Six, six, six." She threw. Two. "I didn't blow enough!" she cried. On the third turn, she rolled a six and shrieked, "See! My blowing works!" Sudha miss smiled. "Shall we try? Everyone roll without blowing." The children rolled. Some got sixes. Neelam looked puzzled. "The dice doesn't know about my blowing?" "The dice doesn't know anything," Sudha miss said.

qa.q: How many times did Neelam blow on the dice the first time?
qa.a: She blew on it three times.

qa.q: Why did Neelam shriek "See! My blowing works!"?
qa.a: She felt excited and powerful, believing her blowing had made the six happen.

qa.q: How did Sudha miss help Neelam, and how could other adults do the same?
qa.a: She had everyone roll without blowing so Neelam could see sixes still came; adults can gently let children test their rituals.

qa.q: How might the other children feel rolling sixes without blowing?
qa.a: They might feel pleased and surprised, and it shows Neelam that the dice isn't listening to anyone.

grounding: Shows a young child at a Diwali party believing that blowing on the dice can make it roll a six.

passage:
Lohri, first day. Kites filled the sky over Amritsar. Baljeet stood beside his cousin Asif, fingers crossed so hard they hurt. Asif's kite won. "It was my fingers!" Baljeet shouted.
Second day. Baljeet crossed his fingers tighter and hopped on one leg. Asif's kite got cut. Baljeet cried. "I didn't hop enough."
Third day. Asif gave him the spool. "No fingers, no hopping. Just watch." The wind pulled the kite left, then right. It won one fight and lost one. "The wind decides a lot," Asif said. "So I'm not in charge?" "Not of the wind."

qa.q: What did Baljeet say when Asif's kite won on the first day?
qa.a: "It was my fingers!"

qa.q: Why did Baljeet cry on the second day?
qa.a: He felt sad and guilty, believing the kite was cut because he hadn't hopped enough.

qa.q: What did Asif do that helped Baljeet?
qa.a: He let Baljeet hold the spool and watch without rituals, so he could see the wind deciding wins and losses.

qa.q: How might Asif feel when Baljeet blames himself?
qa.a: Asif probably felt fond and a little worried, wanting Baljeet to stop thinking the kite depended on him.

grounding: Shows a young child during Lohri believing crossed fingers and hopping can make a cousin's kite win.

passage: The monsoon rain had knocked out the power, and the Ludo game went on by torchlight. Chaitanya needed a six. He pressed the dice to his forehead and whispered, "Please, please." Six! "It helped!" he shouted. Next roll, he pressed again. Three. His lip shook. "I didn't press hard enough." His older cousin Amandeep held up the torch. "Experiment. Ten rolls with your forehead, ten without." They counted sixes by torchlight: two with, two without. Chaitanya stared at the dice. "It's the same." Amandeep grinned. "The dice can't feel your forehead."

qa.q: How many sixes did Chaitanya get with the forehead and without?
qa.a: Two with, two without.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling when he rolled a three?
qa.a: He felt upset and guilty, lip shaking, believing he hadn't pressed the dice hard enough.

qa.q: How did Amandeep help Chaitanya test his belief?
qa.a: He suggested ten rolls with and ten without the forehead press, so Chaitanya could see the ritual didn't change the dice.

qa.q: How might Amandeep see Chaitanya's forehead ritual?
qa.a: Amandeep sees it as sweet but pointless, and turns it into a fun experiment instead of simply telling Chaitanya off.

grounding: Shows a young child during a monsoon power cut believing that pressing the dice to his forehead makes it roll a six.

passage: On the morning of the Class 6 half-yearly exam in the government school at Jalna, Tanuja opened her pencil box and froze. The blue pen was gone. Her lucky pen. She had written every good test with it since Class 4. Without it, her hands went cold. "I'll fail," she whispered to Alka on the bench. "It's just a pen," Alka said, holding out a spare one. Tanuja shook her head. The bell rang. The papers came. For the first ten minutes she couldn't read the questions properly; her heart was too loud. Then she forced herself to start with Alka's pen. She knew the answers. They were in her head, not in the pen. She walked out tired, and feeling almost silly.

qa.q: What had Tanuja written every good test with since Class 4?
qa.a: The blue pen, her lucky pen.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when she found the pen was gone?
qa.a: She felt panicked, hands cold and heart loud, sure she would fail without her lucky pen.

qa.q: What could Tanuja remind herself before the next exam?
qa.a: That the answers are in her head, not in the pen, so any pen will do and she can focus on what she studied.

qa.q: How does Alka see the lost pen?
qa.a: Alka sees it as just a pen and calmly offers a spare, not sharing Tanuja's worry.

grounding: Shows a child believing her lucky pen affects her exam results and feeling real anxiety when it goes missing.

passage: Amara always wore the same yellow socks for football matches in Nairobi. Unwashed, never changed, stuffed in the corner of her bag. Her team had won four games in a row with those socks. On Saturday morning, she opened her bag at the pitch. No socks. Her mother had washed them. Amara's stomach dropped. "We're going to lose," she told Marek, the goalkeeper. "It's my fault." Marek shrugged. "I wear the same gloves every time and we lost twice last month." Amara didn't hear him. She played the first half badly, looking at her white socks, missing passes. At half-time, the coach sat beside her. "What wins matches?" Amara mumbled, "Passing. Running." "Can socks do that?" Amara thought about it. In the second half she played properly. They drew, one-all.

qa.q: What colour were Amara's match socks?
qa.a: Yellow.

qa.q: Why did Amara play the first half badly?
qa.a: She felt anxious and guilty, convinced the missing socks would make the team lose and distracted by worrying about them.

qa.q: How did the coach help Amara at half-time?
qa.a: The coach asked what really wins matches, passing and running, which turned her attention back to what she controls.

qa.q: How does Marek see lucky kit?
qa.a: Marek doesn't trust it much, since he wears the same gloves and they still lost twice last month.

grounding: Shows a child who believes her unwashed match socks affect results and feels real anxiety when they go missing.

passage: At the chess club in the Pune community centre, Chaitanya always sat at table seven, by the window. He had won every tournament game from that seat. On Sunday he arrived and a new boy was already sitting there. Chaitanya stood frozen. The organiser, Bhavna didi, pointed to table three. "Sit there, games start in two minutes." "I can't," Chaitanya whispered. "Table seven is my table." His chest was tight. He sat at table three, but he kept glancing at the window. He lost in twenty moves. "Wrong table," he told Bhavna didi afterwards, eyes wet. She took out his scoresheet. "Look at move eight. You didn't see my bishop. That's not the table." Chaitanya read it twice. Next week he asked to sit at a different table on purpose.

qa.q: Which table did Chaitanya always sit at?
qa.a: Table seven, by the window.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling when he saw the new boy at table seven?
qa.a: He felt panicked and tight in the chest, sure he couldn't win without his usual seat.

qa.q: How did Bhavna didi help, and what did Chaitanya try next?
qa.a: She showed him the real mistake on his scoresheet; next week he chose a different table on purpose to test the belief.

qa.q: How might the new boy at table seven feel if he knew?
qa.a: The new boy would probably be surprised, having no idea the seat meant so much to Chaitanya.

grounding: Shows a child who believes his special seat affects his chess results and feels real anxiety when he cannot use it.

passage:
Saturday.
Diwali tambola at our society tonight. Tickets were given free to every family. Mummy picked up one for me from the pile, but I refused it. I had to choose my own. I spent ten minutes going through the stack looking for one with my birthday number, 17, and my lucky 7. I'm Raghav, the boy with the lucky numbers, everyone knows. Chinmay just grabbed the top one.
Chinmay won the first line.
I didn't win anything.
Later I told Papa it wasn't fair, I had chosen so carefully. He asked, "Does the caller know which ticket you picked?" Obviously not. "So does choosing change which numbers come out?" I didn't want to answer that. But it doesn't. Chinmay's random ticket had the same chance as mine.

qa.q: What did Chinmay win at the tambola?
qa.a: Chinmay won the first line.

qa.q: Why did Raghav spend ten minutes choosing his ticket?
qa.a: He felt hopeful and in control, believing that picking his birthday and lucky numbers would improve his chances.

qa.q: What did Papa's question help Raghav see, and how could he use it next time?
qa.a: That the caller doesn't know which ticket he chose, so choosing changes nothing; next time he can just take any ticket and enjoy the game.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see his win?
qa.a: Chinmay probably sees it as pure luck and fun, since he just grabbed the top ticket.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows him believing that choosing his own tambola ticket with lucky numbers gives him better odds.

passage: At the temple fair in Thrissur, the youth club was running a lucky draw: fifty coupons, one prize, a new bicycle. Jomon had saved his pocket money for weeks. "I'm choosing my own number," he told Harish, pushing through the crowd to the stall. The man held out a box of folded coupons. "Take any." Jomon shook his head. "Can I have number 14? It's my birthday." The man laughed and searched until he found it. Jomon held it tight, sure the bicycle was his. Harish took one without looking. "Why didn't you choose?" Jomon asked. "What's the difference?" Harish said. "One ticket gets pulled. Every ticket is one out of fifty." At eight o'clock the draw was announced. Number 31. Neither of them. Jomon was quiet the whole bus ride home.

qa.q: How many coupons were in the lucky draw?
qa.a: Fifty coupons, one prize.

qa.q: Why did Jomon insist on number 14?
qa.a: He felt excited and in control, believing his birthday number would make the draw more likely to pick him.

qa.q: What could Jomon think about before the next lucky draw?
qa.a: That every coupon, chosen or not, is one out of fifty, so choosing a number doesn't change his chances.

qa.q: How does Harish see choosing a coupon?
qa.a: Harish sees it as making no difference, since every ticket has the same chance whether chosen or not.

grounding: Shows a teenager believing that picking his own lucky-draw number at a fair gives him better odds than a random coupon.

passage: I'm Vishal, and last year, in my second year of college, I thought I'd cracked the online card game. I had a system: sit at the right table, fold a lot, bet big on certain hands. The first week I won a little, and it felt like proof. Then I started losing. Each time, I doubled the next bet, sure my system would win it back. My skill had to beat luck eventually. By October I had used up the money Papa sent for hostel fees. I stopped answering my friend Vaibhav's calls because I didn't want him to ask. He came to my room anyway and sat on my bed. "Show me the app," he said quietly. I did. He didn't lecture. He sat with me while I called the helpline number on the college notice board, and the next morning walked me to the counsellor.

qa.q: What did Vishal use up by October?
qa.a: The money Papa sent for hostel fees.

qa.q: Why did Vishal keep doubling his bets after losing?
qa.a: Vishal felt confident and in control, believing his system and skill would beat luck and win the losses back.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do, and why did it help?
qa.a: He came without lecturing, looked at the app with Vishal, sat with him while he called the helpline and took him to the counsellor, so Vishal got real help.

qa.q: What was it like for Vaibhav when Vishal stopped answering his calls?
qa.a: Vaibhav was probably worried, which is why he came to the room anyway and quietly asked to see the app.

grounding: A young adult looks back on believing his system could beat an online card game, doubling after losses, until a friend helped him get support.

passage:
College counsellor's note, 9 February.
Saurabh, second-year commerce, came in today with his sister Sarita, who had asked for the appointment. Over three months he has been doing day-trading on his phone with money from his part-time job and a loan from a friend. He showed me a notebook of rules he calls his "system." He believes his chart reading gives him control, and that after each loss he must trade bigger to recover. His losses have grown each week.
He was defensive at first. When Sarita said she had heard him awake at 3 a.m. checking prices, he went quiet.
We agreed today: he will delete the app with Sarita present, and he will meet a financial counsellor from the helpline I gave him. I will see him again on Friday.

qa.q: Who asked for Saurabh's appointment with the counsellor?
qa.a: His sister Sarita.

qa.q: What does Saurabh's notebook of rules suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels in control and confident, believing his chart-reading system can beat what are really random price swings.

qa.q: What steps were agreed, and why are they helpful?
qa.a: Deleting the app with Sarita present and meeting a financial counsellor from the helpline, which remove the temptation and bring in expert support.

qa.q: How might Sarita have felt hearing Saurabh awake at 3 a.m.?
qa.a: Sarita was likely very worried about her brother, which is why she arranged the appointment and came with him.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a young adult believing his trading system can beat randomness and trading bigger after losses.

passage:
Tuesday.
Lost again on the colour game tonight. Red came up six times in a row and I kept betting black, doubling each time. My system is simple: double after every loss, so one win covers everything. It has to work. I'm Nilesh, the maths topper, a boy who understands numbers. So why am I down more than two months of my tuition earnings?
Wednesday.
Couldn't sleep. Checked the app at 4 a.m. Lost more. My hands were shaking.
Thursday.
Told Lakshmi didi everything. I expected shouting. She just put her hand on mine and said, "This isn't about your maths. These games are built to win." She sat with me while I deleted the app, and she called a helpline for young people with gambling problems. I have an appointment tomorrow. I feel ashamed. But also like I can breathe.

qa.q: What colour came up six times in a row on Tuesday night?
qa.a: Red came up six times in a row.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling by Thursday?
qa.a: He felt ashamed but relieved, able to breathe after finally telling Lakshmi didi everything.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi didi do, and why was it the right response?
qa.a: She listened without shouting, explained the games are built to win, sat with him as he deleted the app, and called a helpline the same day.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi didi have felt hearing the whole story?
qa.a: Lakshmi didi was probably shocked and worried, but chose to stay calm and supportive rather than angry.

grounding: A young adult's diary shows him believing his doubling system can beat a random game, until he tells his sister and gets help.

passage: Last spring I had three final-round interviews in two weeks, and I'm writing down how I got through them because Farida asked. I'm Rukmini, a woman who used to blame herself for everything. Before each interview I drew two columns. What I control: my preparation, my examples, sleeping properly, arriving early. What I don't: the panel's mood, who else applied, whether they'd already chosen someone internal. I put all my effort into the first column. I practised answers out loud. I didn't wear my "lucky" earrings, and I didn't read my horoscope. When I didn't get the first job, I looked at the first column. Had I done my part? Yes. The rest was not mine to carry. I got the third job. I don't think I was luckier; I just kept working on what was mine.

qa.q: How many final-round interviews did Rukmini have in two weeks?
qa.a: Three final-round interviews.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when the first job went to someone else?
qa.a: Rukmini felt disappointed but calm, able to accept it without self-blame after checking that her own part had been done.

qa.q: Why is Rukmini's two-column method wise?
qa.a: It puts effort into what she controls and accepts the random rest without superstition or self-blame.

qa.q: How might Farida see Rukmini's story?
qa.a: Farida, who asked how Rukmini got through, may see that calm comes from separating effort from luck, not from being fearless.

grounding: A young professional describes separating what she controls from luck, working hard on her part and accepting the rest without superstition or self-blame.

passage:
Coach's note, state badminton trials, Sunday.
Ira lost her quarter-final 19–21 in the third game. A net cord shot fell on her side at 19–all. Last year, a loss like that sent her into a week of blaming herself, or blaming the hall, or buying a new lucky wristband.
Today was different. Afterwards she sat with me and made two lists, on her own. What she controlled: her serve under pressure (weak), her footwork in the third game (good), her decision to play safe at 18. What she didn't: the net cord, the lighting, the draw. "I'll work on the serve," she said. "The net cord was just luck."
No wristband talk. No self-blame. I've added extra serving practice to her plan for next week.
Irawati

qa.q: What was the score of Ira's third game?
qa.a: She lost her quarter-final 19–21 in the third game.

qa.q: How can you tell Ira felt steadier after this loss than last year?
qa.a: She calmly sorted what she controlled from what she didn't and called the net cord "just luck", with no self-blame or lucky wristband.

qa.q: What will change in Ira's training, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Extra serving practice, because the serve was the weak part she controls, while the net cord was random.

qa.q: How might Irawati, the coach, feel watching Ira make the lists on her own?
qa.a: Irawati seems pleased and proud, noting the change from last year's self-blame and superstition.

grounding: A coach's note shows a young athlete separating what she controlled from luck after a loss, working on her serve and accepting the net cord.

passage:
Friday night.
The monsoon failed again this year, and half my tomato crop at the farm dried up. I'm Mehak, and three years ago this would have broken me. I'd have said I was cursed, or tied a lemon to the gate like my neighbour does.
This time I sat with a notebook. What I controlled: I chose drought-tolerant seeds for half the field (those survived), I set up the drip lines, I kept records. What I didn't: the rain, the heat, the price at the mandi. Lalit bhaiya, who farms next to me, says I should do a puja for rain. I told him he can, and I'll join if he likes. But I also told him I'm switching the whole field to the tougher seeds next year and digging the second farm pond. That's mine to do. The rain isn't.

qa.q: What did Mehak choose for half the field?
qa.a: Drought-tolerant seeds for half the field.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling about the failed monsoon this time?
qa.a: Mehak felt disappointed but steady, not cursed or broken, because of looking calmly at what was and wasn't under Mehak's control.

qa.q: What are Mehak's plans for next year, and why are they wise?
qa.a: Switching the whole field to tougher seeds and digging a second pond, putting effort where Mehak has control instead of blaming luck.

qa.q: How does Lalit bhaiya seem to see the failed rain?
qa.a: Lalit bhaiya sees rain as something to pray for, and Mehak respects that while also acting on what can be controlled.

grounding: A young farmer's diary shows separating skill from luck, investing effort in what can be controlled and accepting the failed rain without superstition or self-blame.

passage: In the Class 5 maths period at the Nashik school, Arohi ma'am handed out coins for a probability experiment. "Flip ten times and write down each result." Divyansh flipped. Heads. Heads. Heads. Heads. Heads. The whole bench leaned in. "Next one has to be tails," Divyansh announced. "It's been heads too many times. It has to balance." He was so sure he bet his friend an eraser. He flipped. Heads again. "No way!" Arohi ma'am came over. "Divyansh, does the coin remember the last five flips?" He looked at the coin. "It... doesn't have a brain." "So what are the chances for the next flip?" He thought hard. "Half and half. Same as always." He handed over the eraser, grumbling, but grinning a little.

qa.q: How many heads did Divyansh flip in a row before the sixth flip?
qa.a: Five heads.

qa.q: Why was Divyansh so sure the next flip would be tails?
qa.a: He felt excited and certain that the coin had to balance itself after so many heads, as if chance had a memory.

qa.q: How did Arohi ma'am help Divyansh see his mistake?
qa.a: She asked whether the coin remembers the last flips, which led him to see each flip is half and half on its own.

qa.q: How might the friend who won the eraser feel?
qa.a: The friend was probably pleased and amused, since Divyansh had been so sure.

grounding: Shows a child believing tails must come after five heads because chance balances itself out, until his teacher asks whether the coin remembers.

passage:
Monday. In the gully cricket match, Gautam lost the toss with heads. He called heads again on Tuesday and lost. "Tomorrow tails is due," Bhupen said. "No," said Gautam. "Heads is due. It's been tails twice."
Wednesday. Tails again. Gautam kicked the stumps. Three tails! He was sure the coin was now "full of tails" and heads had to come.
Friday. Bhupen's elder brother, home from college, watched Gautam call. "Heads, it's due!" Tails. Gautam groaned. The brother picked up the coin and flipped it twenty times on the step, counting out loud. Heads, tails, tails, heads, heads, heads... It came out eleven and nine. "It doesn't keep a list," he said. "Every flip is new." Gautam stared at the coin, then called tails, just to see.

qa.q: How many times did the brother flip the coin on the step?
qa.a: Twenty times, and it came out eleven and nine.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling on Wednesday when tails came again?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and sure that heads had to come next, kicking the stumps because the coin wasn't balancing out.

qa.q: What did the brother's experiment show, and how could Gautam use it?
qa.a: That the coin doesn't keep a list and every flip is new; Gautam can stop expecting a result to be due.

qa.q: How does Bhupen see the tosses early in the week?
qa.a: Bhupen also thinks a result can be due, just picking tails instead of heads.

grounding: Shows over a week a child believing heads must come after several tails, as if chance remembers and balances itself.

passage: Raghav, you've flipped that coin nine times and you're sure the next one must be tails? Let your Farhan Dada tell you about the marble game in our lane in Bhopal, when I was your age. We played odds and evens with a fistful of marbles. My friend always guessed. Seven times in a row, it was evens. I was certain the next had to be odds. "It's due!" I said. I bet my best cat's-eye marble. Evens. I bet two more. Evens again. By evening I had lost my whole tin. I went home crying. Dear Jatin,
I'm writing because I didn't know how to say this at the café without it turning into an argument.
Over the last month, I've watched you bet on the horse races every weekend. First small, then more after each loss. On Saturday you said, "My luck has to turn now, I've lost six times," and you put in your whole month's savings. I saw your hands when the result came.
I'm not writing to explain probability to you. You know it better than I do. I'm writing because you're my oldest friend, practically my brother, and I'm worried. You've stopped coming to cricket. You look tired.
There's a counselling service for betting problems near your office. I've put the number at the end. If you want, I'll come with you the first time. No lecture. Just coffee after.
Your friend,
Sahil
